```{r confirmcov, fig.cap="Inference for the revised SIMEX. Coverage of each target by the interval built for it, with Wilson 95\\% intervals over 500 replicates. The dashed line is at 0.95. Rows are studies and columns are a target and an interval. The quadratic $q_2$ and the true $M$ are known only in the closed-form designs, and the first two columns use a narrower coverage scale. The pointwise interval for $q_2(t^*)$ uses the SE with the first-step adjustment. The known covariance (circles) and cross-fitted calibration (triangles) share data and folds.", out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/fig_confirm_coverage.pdf")
```

For regression calibration, the third amendment uses the covariate-shape design of Section \ref{sec:designs} with $n\in\{1000,5000\}$. Treating the calibration as fixed understates the variance of regression calibration, and the first-step adjustment of Proposition \ref{prop:rcfold} removes most of the shortfall where the target of regression calibration is the ATT (Figure \ref{fig:rccov}). In the Gaussian cells, the adjustment carried `r pr(gc, "rc_fold", "calibration_var_share", 0)`% of the variance of the combined influence value. With the lasso learner, a lasso on the covariates and their squares (the lasso with squares), coverage rose from `r srng(gc, "rc_fold", "cover_att_fixedse")` with the SE that treats the calibration as fixed to `r srng(gc, "rc_fold", "cover_att")` with the first-step adjustment. At $n=5{,}000$ it was `r srng(gc5, "rc_fold", "cover_att")`, with a ratio of mean SE to empirical SD of `r srng(gc5, "rc_fold", "se_ratio", d = 2)`. With the parametric learner, for which the gradient in (C.18) is exact, coverage was `r fmt(sv("gauss_linear_n1000", "rc_fold", "cover_att", le = "glm"))` at $n=1{,}000$ and `r fmt(sv("gauss_linear_n5000", "rc_fold", "cover_att", le = "glm"))` at $n=5{,}000$.

The first-step adjustment is much larger for regression calibration than for SIMEX, whose adjustment carried at most `r fmt(100 * sx_share, 1)`% of the variance in any cell of the third amendment and `r fmt(simex_share("all"), 1)`% in any cell of the first to fifth. Regression calibration estimates more of the calibration. SIMEX needs only the error variance $s$, whereas regression calibration also needs the mean and covariance of $Z$ within each treatment group, which fix the slope of its predictor. After the study, we split the first-step adjustment by component in the closed-form design at $n=200{,}000$. Relative to the variance of the DR-DiD influence value, the group-covariance part contributed `r vshare("linear", "cov")`%, the group-mean part `r vshare("linear", "mean")`% and the error-variance part `r vshare("linear", "s")`% with a linear trend and the parametric learner. With a quadratic trend and the lasso learner, the shares were `r vshare("quad", "cov")`%, `r vshare("quad", "mean")`% and `r vshare("quad", "s")`%. The parts are correlated, so these shares do not add up to the adjustment's total.

Some under-coverage remains at $n=1{,}000$, where the ratio of mean SE to empirical SD was `r srng(gc1, "rc_fold", "se_ratio", d = 2)`. Outliers do not explain it, because the excess kurtosis of the estimates was `r nm(vt_k[1], 2)` to `r nm(vt_k[2], 2)`. The higher-order terms of the calibration, which the first-order expansion omits and which matter with about 400 treated units per sample, may explain it, but we have not verified this. Where the conditions of Proposition \ref{prop:rcfold} fail, the adjustment does not rescue the intervals. In the log-normal cells, where no polynomial learner is consistent for the control regression, the ratio of mean SE to empirical SD was `r srng(c(ll, lq1, lq5), "rc_fold", "se_ratio", d = 2)`. In the three cells of the original design, where measurement error moved the estimate by only `r fmt(min(abs(dnl)))`--`r fmt(max(abs(dnl)))` (against about 0.4 in the Gaussian cells), the adjustment carried `r fmt(100 * min(dsh), 1)`--`r fmt(100 * max(dsh), 1)`% of the variance and changed coverage by at most `r fmt(max(abs(dcd)))`. The SE with the first-step adjustment costs no extra fit, because it uses the saved influence values and the gradient of the fitted outcome regression.

```{r rccov, fig.cap="Coverage of the ATT by regression calibration with cross-fitted calibration, with the SE that treats the calibration as fixed (triangles) and with the SE that includes the first-step adjustment of Proposition \\ref{prop:rcfold} (circles). Wilson 95\\% intervals over 500 replicates per cell. The dashed line is at 0.95. The Gaussian and log-normal cells at reliability 0.6 and at reliability 0.9 are those of Sections \\ref{sec:inference} and \\ref{sec:accuracy}, and the original-design cells have classical error and nonlinear trends.", out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/fig_rc_coverage.pdf")
```

## Accuracy under classical error {#sec:accuracy}

In the original study, classical covariate error biased every adjusted estimator, and the bias grew as reliability fell (Figure \ref{fig:simbias}). The original SIMEX corrections roughly halved the bias of their naive counterparts but did not remove it. Paired on the same replicates at reliability 0.6, $n=5{,}000$ and nonlinear trends, SIMEX-lasso reduced the mean squared error by `r with(ex$prod$paired, fmt(-mse_difference[cell_id=="x_classical__r0.60__nonlinear__N5000" & corrected=="simex_lasso" & basis=="clean"]*1e3, 2))` $\times10^{-3}$ (paired MCSE `r with(ex$prod$paired, fmt(mse_difference_mcse[cell_id=="x_classical__r0.60__nonlinear__N5000" & corrected=="simex_lasso" & basis=="clean"]*1e3, 2))` $\times10^{-3}$). The remaining bias is the extrapolation error that Section \ref{sec:biasint} bounds.

```{r simbias, fig.cap="Bias under classical covariate error in the original study, by reliability. A reliability of 1 is the error-free baseline cell, which was generated with different seeds and so is not paired with the error cells. Error bars are $\\pm2$ MCSE over 500 replicates. Dashed lines are the original SIMEX corrections with known reliability.", out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/fig_sim_bias.pdf")
```

The same-sample comparison shows that the bias due to measurement error barely depended on the learner. With $n=5{,}000$, the difference between DR-DiD fitted to the error-prone covariates and to the true covariates of the same replicates was `r gap(oc_x[2], "dml_lasso")` for the lasso and `r gap(oc_x[2], "dml_xgb")` for boosting under classical error at reliability 0.6 with nonlinear trends, and `r gap(oc_x[1], "dml_lasso")` and `r gap(oc_x[1], "dml_xgb")` with linear trends. Under large misclassification it was between `r nm(min(og$value[og$cell %in% oc_m]))` and `r nm(max(og$value[og$cell %in% oc_m]))`. Paired MCSEs were at most `r fmt(max(og$mcse), 4)`. Boosting's additional bias, `r nm(co(oc_x[2], "dml_xgb", "latent"))` on the true covariates with nonlinear trends, is learner bias that remains without measurement error. On the true covariates, lasso DR-DiD covered the sample ATT in `r orng(ocov(c(oc_x, oc_m), "dml_lasso", "latent"))` of replicates. On the error-prone covariates it covered it in `r orng(ocov(oc_x, "dml_lasso", "observed"))` under covariate error and `r orng(ocov(oc_m, "dml_lasso", "observed"))` under misclassification.

The second amendment, specified after the results of the original study and the first amendment had been seen (Appendix \ref{app:repro}), compares SIMEX with the regression calibration of Section \ref{sec:rcmethod}. In this study the calibration was computed once on the full sample, and the SE treated it as fixed, as the original SIMEX did. Each replicate also refits DR-DiD on the reported covariates (the naive estimator) and on the true covariates.

The comparison ran in three settings. The first is the closed-form design of Section \ref{sec:designs}, where the best linear predictor is the conditional mean, the trend is linear and regression calibration is exact. The second is the twelve classical-error cells of the original study. The third is the two cells with large differential covariate error, where both corrections assume the wrong error model. Seeds and folds match the earlier studies, so every replicate pairs with a saved SIMEX fit. Each cell has 500 replicates. No fit failed, and no latent variance needed the pre-specified floor.

Under classical error in the original design, regression calibration removed the bias due to measurement error, and SIMEX did not (Table \ref{tab:rc}). At reliability 0.6 with nonlinear trends and $n=5{,}000$, the bias against the sample ATT was `r nm(rcd(c6, "naive", "bias_att"))` for the naive estimator, `r nm(rcd(c6, "rc_group", "bias_att"))` after regression calibration, `r nm(rcd(c6, "simex_production", "bias_att"))` for the original SIMEX-lasso and `r nm(rcd(c6, "latent", "bias_att"))` on the true covariates (MCSE at most `r fmt(max(rcL$mcse[rcL$study == "rc_dgp" & rcL$cell == c6 & rcL$metric == "bias_att"]), 4)`). In all twelve cells, the regression-calibrated estimate differed from the estimate on the true covariates of the same replicate by less than two paired MCSEs (largest difference `r fmt(max(abs(p_l$est_diff)), 4)`). Regression calibration also had a smaller mean absolute error than the original SIMEX-lasso in all twelve cells, by `r fmt(min(-p_s$abs_err_diff), 4)` to `r fmt(max(-p_s$abs_err_diff), 4)`, and by more than two paired MCSEs in `r num_word(sum(-p_s$abs_err_diff > 2 * p_s$abs_err_diff_mcse))` of them. The difference averaged `r fmt(mean(-p_s$abs_err_diff[n1k]), 4)` at $n=1{,}000$ and `r fmt(mean(-p_s$abs_err_diff[!n1k]), 4)` at $n=5{,}000$. At $n=1{,}000$, SIMEX had the larger empirical SD in `r of_six(sum(sd1k("simex_production") > sd1k("rc_group")))`. Regression calibration covered the sample ATT in `r dgp_rng("rc_group", "cover_att")` of replicates, against `r dgp_rng("simex_production", "cover_att")` for SIMEX.

In the closed-form design, regression calibration was close to unbiased, with bias `r g_rng("rc_group", "bias_att", signed = TRUE)` (MCSE at most `r fmt(max(rcL$mcse[rcL$study == "rc_gauss" & rcL$method == "rc_group" & rcL$metric == "bias_att"]), 4)`). SIMEX with cross-fitted calibration kept the extrapolation error $q_2(-1)-\tau=0.16$ of Section \ref{sec:inference}, with bias `r g_rng("simex_fold", "bias_att", signed = TRUE)`. The intervals of regression calibration under-covered, however. The SE that treats the calibration as fixed was `r g_rng("rc_group", "se_ratio", d = 2)` of the empirical SD, and coverage was `r g_rng("rc_group", "cover_att")`. At $n=1{,}000$ the empirical SD of the regression-calibrated estimate was `r fmt(rcg("gauss_r0.60_n1000", "rc_group", "emp_sd"))`, against `r fmt(rcg("gauss_r0.60_n1000", "latent", "emp_sd"))` on the true covariates. Its RMSE, `r fmt(rcg("gauss_r0.60_n1000", "rc_group", "rmse"))`, was still below that of SIMEX, `r fmt(rcg("gauss_r0.60_n1000", "simex_fold", "rmse"))`. With cross-fitted calibration, the first-step adjustment of Proposition \ref{prop:rcfold} removes most of this shortfall (Section \ref{sec:inference}).

In these designs regression calibration was the better point correction. It used the same information as SIMEX, needed no extrapolation, and matched the fit on the true covariates. Within each treatment group, the error-prone covariates of the original design are close to Gaussian, which is the case in which regression calibration is exact (Section \ref{sec:gap}). They are drawn as Gaussian, apart from household size, which is a rounded and truncated Gaussian, and treatment depends on them through a logit-linear propensity (Appendix \ref{app:computation}). After the study, we estimated the relative excess calibration error of each of them within each treatment group, using 20,000 draws per group. At reliability 0.6 the estimate was at most `r fmt(max(gor$gap_share[gor$covariate != "c4"]), 4)` for the four Gaussian covariates, which is within the resolution of the estimator for Gaussian samples of the same size (at most `r fmt(max(gor$gaussian_resolution), 4)`), and `r fmt(max(gor$gap_share[gor$covariate == "c4"]), 3)` for household size. In the log-normal designs of Section \ref{sec:map} it is `r fmt(gpm(0.25, 0.6), 3)` to `r fmt(gpm(1, 0.6), 3)` at the same reliability.

```{r rc}
rc_sel <- data.frame(
  study = c(rep("rc_gauss", 2), rep("rc_dgp", 4), rep("rc_xnc", 2)),
  cell = c("gauss_r0.60_n1000", "gauss_r0.60_n5000", "x_classical__r0.60__nonlinear__N1000",
           "x_classical__r0.60__nonlinear__N5000", "x_classical__r0.75__nonlinear__N5000",
           "x_classical__r0.90__nonlinear__N5000", "x_nc__large__linear__N5000", "x_nc__large__nonlinear__N5000"),
  learner = c("glm", "glm", rep("glmnet", 6)),
  simex = c("simex_fold", "simex_fold", rep("simex_production", 6)),
  Design = c("Closed form, $n=1{,}000$", "Closed form, $n=5{,}000$", "Classical, $r=0.6$, $n=1{,}000$",
             "Classical, $r=0.6$, $n=5{,}000$", "Classical, $r=0.75$, $n=5{,}000$", "Classical, $r=0.9$, $n=5{,}000$",
             "Differential, linear", "Differential, nonlinear"))
rc_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(rc_sel)), function(i) {
  s <- rc_sel[i, ]; g <- \(me, mt) rv(s$study, s$cell, s$learner, me, mt)
  data.frame(Design = s$Design,
             b_n = fmt(g("naive", "bias_att")), b_rc = fmt(g("rc_group", "bias_att")),
             b_s = fmt(g(s$simex, "bias_att")), b_l = fmt(g("latent", "bias_att")),
             r_rc = fmt(g("rc_group", "rmse")), r_s = fmt(g(s$simex, "rmse")),
             c_rc = fmt(g("rc_group", "cover_att")), c_s = fmt(g(s$simex, "cover_att")))
}))
mc_max <- function(st) fmt(max(rcL$mcse[rcL$study %in% st & rcL$metric == "bias_att" &
                                        rcL$cell %in% rc_sel$cell]), 3)
kbl2(rc_tab, font = 7.5, escape = FALSE, align = "lrrrrrrrr",
     col.names = c("Design", "Naive", "RC", "SIMEX", "True", "RC", "SIMEX", "RC", "SIMEX"),
     sprintf(paste("Regression calibration (RC) and SIMEX given the same information (second amendment), 500 replicates per cell.",
                   "The closed-form rows have reliability 0.6 known, a parametric learner and SIMEX with cross-fitted calibration at $M=0$ (Section \\ref{sec:inference}).",
                   "The other rows use the original design, the lasso learner and the original SIMEX-lasso. The classical rows have nonlinear trends,",
                   "and the differential rows have large error and $n=5{,}000$, with both corrections assuming reliability 0.75.",
                   "Bias is against the sample ATT, and its MCSE is at most %s in the closed-form rows and %s elsewhere. True is the estimator on the true covariates.",
                   "Coverage of nominal 95\\%% intervals has MCSE of about 0.01 near 0.95. All cells, with paired contrasts, are in Appendix \\ref{app:rc}."),
             mc_max("rc_gauss"), mc_max(c("rc_dgp", "rc_xnc")))) |>
  add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "Bias" = 4, "RMSE" = 2, "Coverage" = 2))
```

The covariate-shape design of the third amendment (Section \ref{sec:designs}) asks whether the ranking survives a design in which the linear predictor of regression calibration is not the conditional mean. By Proposition \ref{prop:gap}, the calibration gap is zero in its Gaussian cells and not in its log-normal cells. Both corrections use cross-fitted calibration, the lasso with squares as the learner, and the known reliability 0.6 (Table \ref{tab:shape}).

Where its linear predictor was the conditional mean, regression calibration was again the better correction. In the four Gaussian cells its bias ranged from `r srng(gc, "rc_fold", "bias_att", signed = TRUE)` (MCSE at most `r fmt(mx(gc, "rc_fold", "bias_att", "mcse"), 4)`), while SIMEX's ranged from `r srng(gc, "simex_fold", "bias_att", signed = TRUE)`, the extrapolation error of the quadratic. With log-normal covariates and a linear trend, regression calibration was close to unbiased, with bias `r nm(sv(ll[1], "rc_fold", "bias_att"))` at $n=1{,}000$ and `r nm(sv(ll[2], "rc_fold", "bias_att"))` (MCSE `r fmt(sv(ll[2], "rc_fold", "bias_att", col = "mcse"))`) at $n=5{,}000$. SIMEX's bias in those two cells was `r nm(sv(ll[1], "simex_fold", "bias_att"))` and `r nm(sv(ll[2], "simex_fold", "bias_att"))`. Across these six cells, regression calibration had the smaller mean absolute error, by `r fmt(min(aed))` to `r fmt(max(aed))` (paired MCSE at most `r fmt(max(aem))`).

Skewed covariates combined with a nonlinear trend broke both corrections, in opposite directions. With log-normal covariates and a quadratic trend, the bias of regression calibration was `r nm(sv(lq1, "rc_fold", "bias_att"))` at $n=1{,}000$ and `r nm(sv(lq5, "rc_fold", "bias_att"))` at $n=5{,}000$, and that of SIMEX was `r nm(sv(lq1, "simex_fold", "bias_att"))` and `r nm(sv(lq5, "simex_fold", "bias_att"))`. The ATT is 0.5, and the naive bias was `r nm(sv(lq1, "naive", "bias_att"))` and `r nm(sv(lq5, "naive", "bias_att"))`. SIMEX had the smaller mean absolute error at $n=5{,}000$, by `r fmt(sp(lq5, "rc_fold - simex_fold", "abs_err_diff"))` (paired MCSE `r fmt(sp(lq5, "rc_fold - simex_fold", "abs_err_diff_mcse"))`). At $n=1{,}000$ the difference was `r fmt(sp(lq1, "rc_fold - simex_fold", "abs_err_diff"))` (`r fmt(sp(lq1, "rc_fold - simex_fold", "abs_err_diff_mcse"))`), and the empirical SD of regression calibration was `r fmt(sv(lq1, "rc_fold", "emp_sd"), 2)`. Neither interval was reliable in these cells. Regression calibration covered the ATT in `r fmt(sv(lq1, "rc_fold", "cover_att"))` and `r fmt(sv(lq5, "rc_fold", "cover_att"))` of replicates. SIMEX covered it in `r fmt(sv(lq1, "simex_fold", "cover_att"))` and `r fmt(sv(lq5, "simex_fold", "cover_att"))` at $M=0$, and in `r fmt(sv(lq1, "simex_fold", "cover_att_M0.05"))` and `r fmt(sv(lq5, "simex_fold", "cover_att_M0.05"))` at $M=0.05$.

```{r shape}
sh_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(shp_cells)), function(i) {
  ce <- shp_cells$cell[i]; g <- \(me, mt) sv(ce, me, mt)
  data.frame(Design = sprintf("%s, $n=%s$", ifelse(shp_cells$trend[i] == "linear", "linear", "quadratic"),
                              gsub(",", "{,}", big(shp_cells$n[i]))),
             b_n = fmt(g("naive", "bias_att")), b_rc = fmt(g("rc_fold", "bias_att")),
             b_s = fmt(g("simex_fold", "bias_att")), b_l = fmt(g("latent", "bias_att")),
             r_rc = fmt(g("rc_fold", "rmse")), r_s = fmt(g("simex_fold", "rmse")),
             c_rc = fmt(g("rc_fold", "cover_att")), c_rcf = fmt(g("rc_fold", "cover_att_fixedse")),
             c_s = fmt(g("simex_fold", "cover_att")), c_s5 = fmt(g("simex_fold", "cover_att_M0.05")))
}))
sh_mc <- max(a3L$mcse[a3L$study == "shape" & a3L$learner == "glmnet" & a3L$metric == "bias_att"])
kbl2(sh_tab, font = 7.2, escape = FALSE, align = "lrrrrrrrrrr",
     col.names = c("Design", "Naive", "RC", "SIMEX", "True", "RC", "SIMEX", "RC", "RC, fixed", "$M=0$", "$M=0.05$"),
     sprintf(paste("Covariate shape and trend (third amendment). Regression calibration (RC) and SIMEX, both with cross-fitted calibration,",
                   "use the same information, the lasso learner and reliability 0.6 known, with 500 replicates per cell. Bias is against the ATT, 0.5,",
                   "and its MCSE is at most %s. True is the estimator on the true covariates. RC coverage uses the SE with the first-step adjustment of Proposition \\ref{prop:rcfold}",
                   "or the SE that treats the calibration as fixed. SIMEX coverage uses interval (5) with the SE with the first-step adjustment.",
                   "Coverage near 0.95 has MCSE of about 0.01. All metrics and paired contrasts are in Appendix \\ref{app:shape}."),
             fmt(sh_mc, 3))) |>
  add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "Bias" = 4, "RMSE" = 2, "Coverage, RC" = 2, "Coverage, SIMEX" = 2)) |>
  pack_rows(index = c("Gaussian covariates" = 4, "Log-normal covariates" = 4))
```

The fourth amendment ran a design chosen because population calculations made before the study put the target of regression calibration further from the ATT than SIMEX's. Those calculations were later corrected numerically (Appendix \ref{app:repro}), and the corrected values in Section \ref{sec:map} keep the ordering. The true covariates are log-normal with skewness 6.2, and the reliability is 0.9. The amendment also adds a learner close to the nonparametric regressions that the calculations assume, the lasso on natural splines with five degrees of freedom in each continuous covariate. With this spline lasso, a linear trend and $n=5{,}000$, regression calibration had bias `r nm(s4(l9, "glmnet_ns", "rc_fold", "bias_att"))` and SIMEX `r nm(s4(l9, "glmnet_ns", "simex_fold", "bias_att"))` (MCSE at most `r fmt(max(s4(l9, "glmnet_ns", "rc_fold", "bias_att", "mcse"), s4(l9, "glmnet_ns", "simex_fold", "bias_att", "mcse")))`), against population values of `r nm(pmv(1, 0.9, 0, "rc"))` and `r nm(pmv(1, 0.9, 0, "simex"))`. SIMEX had the smaller mean absolute error, by `r fmt(p4(l9, "glmnet_ns", "rc_fold - simex_fold", "abs_err_diff"))` (paired MCSE `r fmt(p4(l9, "glmnet_ns", "rc_fold - simex_fold", "abs_err_diff_mcse"))`). Neither interval was reliable. Regression calibration covered the ATT in `r fmt(s4(l9, "glmnet_ns", "rc_fold", "cover_att"))` of replicates, and SIMEX in `r fmt(s4(l9, "glmnet_ns", "simex_fold", "cover_att"))` at $M=0$ and `r fmt(s4(l9, "glmnet_ns", "simex_fold", "cover_att_M0.05"))` at $M=0.05$. The bound $M=0.05$ is too small for this design. The population extrapolation error of SIMEX is `r fmt(pmv(1, 0.9, 0, "simex"))`, and by the Peano bound the third derivative of its curve must then exceed `r fmt(pmv(1, 0.9, 0, "simex") * 22 / 21, 3)` somewhere on $[-1,2]$.

## Dependence on the outcome learner {#sec:learner}

On the data of the fourth amendment's linear cell with $n=5{,}000$, the learner decided which correction was more accurate. With the lasso with squares, regression calibration had bias `r nm(s4(l9, "glmnet", "rc_fold", "bias_att"))` and SIMEX `r nm(s4(l9, "glmnet", "simex_fold", "bias_att"))`, and regression calibration had the smaller mean absolute error, by `r fmt(-p4(l9, "glmnet", "rc_fold - simex_fold", "abs_err_diff"))` (paired MCSE `r fmt(p4(l9, "glmnet", "rc_fold - simex_fold", "abs_err_diff_mcse"))`). Corollary \ref{cor:rcbias} explains the difference. The spline lasso learns the control group's calibration gap and evaluates it at the treated units' calibrated points. The gap is uncorrelated with linear functions of the observed covariates, so a learner close to linear in the calibrated covariates largely ignores it. In the Gaussian cell at reliability 0.9, where the gap is zero, regression calibration had bias `r nm(s4(g9, "glmnet", "rc_fold", "bias_att"))` and SIMEX `r nm(s4(g9, "glmnet", "simex_fold", "bias_att"))` (MCSE at most `r fmt(max(s4(g9, "glmnet", "rc_fold", "bias_att", "mcse"), s4(g9, "glmnet", "simex_fold", "bias_att", "mcse")), 4)`).

With the spline lasso and a quadratic trend, the cell measured a failure of the learner rather than of either correction. In `r t4(q9, "glmnet_ns", "latent", "n_abs_err_gt1")` of 500 replicates, the estimator on the true covariates erred by more than 1, and its RMSE was `r fmt(s4(q9, "glmnet_ns", "latent", "rmse"), 2)`. A diagnostic run after the study traced these errors to controls whose $W_1$ lay far above the largest value in the training folds, where the spline lasso extrapolates badly and the propensity reaches its clipping bound (Appendix \ref{app:a45}). In the worst replicate, one control with $W_1=`r fmt(r389$top_w1[r389$fold == r389k], 1)`$, against a training maximum of `r fmt(r389$train_max_w1[r389$fold == r389k], 1)`, moved the estimate to `r nm(mean(r389$tau_fold), 1)`. The median errors, which were not a pre-specified metric, were `r nm(t4(q9, "glmnet_ns", "rc_fold", "median_err"))` for regression calibration, `r nm(t4(q9, "glmnet_ns", "simex_fold", "median_err"))` for SIMEX and `r nm(t4(q9, "glmnet_ns", "latent", "median_err"))` on the true covariates.

A fifth amendment refitted the three spline cells with each covariate clamped to its training range before the spline basis is evaluated, so both nuisance fits are constant beyond that range. Clamping bounds the propensity of such a unit but not its outcome residual. In the quadratic cell, `r c5(q9, "latent", "n_big_new")` replicates still gave the estimator on the true covariates an error above 1, and the RMSE of regression calibration fell from `r fmt(c5(q9, "rc_fold", "rmse_old"), 2)` to `r fmt(c5(q9, "rc_fold", "rmse_new"), 2)`. In the linear cell at $n=5{,}000$, the mean error of regression calibration became `r nm(c5(l9, "rc_fold", "mean_err_new"))` and that of SIMEX `r nm(c5(l9, "simex_fold", "mean_err_new"))`, so the ranking stood. The fourth amendment's fits therefore remain the primary results, and the fifth amendment is a sensitivity analysis.

## Differential covariate error {#sec:differential}

When the covariate error is differential with respect to treatment, both corrections assume the wrong error model. In the original study, with large error, nonlinear trends and $n=5{,}000$, SIMEX-lasso increased the bias of lasso DR-DiD from `r v(xnci, "dml_lasso")` to `r v(xnci, "simex_lasso")`, and its coverage was `r v("x_nc__large__nonlinear__N5000","simex_lasso","coverage")`, with a Wilson upper limit of `r v("x_nc__large__nonlinear__N5000","simex_lasso","cov_wilson_hi")`. In the second amendment, both corrections moved the estimate further from the ATT under large differential covariate error. With linear trends the bias was `r nm(rcx("linear", "naive", "bias_att"))` for the naive estimator, `r nm(rcx("linear", "rc_group", "bias_att"))` after regression calibration and `r nm(rcx("linear", "simex_production", "bias_att"))` for SIMEX-lasso. With nonlinear trends it was `r nm(rcx("nonlinear", "naive", "bias_att"))`, `r nm(rcx("nonlinear", "rc_group", "bias_att"))` and `r nm(rcx("nonlinear", "simex_production", "bias_att"))`. No correction covered the ATT in more than `r fmt(max(rcL$value[rcL$study == "rc_xnc" & rcL$method %in% c("rc_group", "simex_production") & rcL$metric == "cover_att"]))` of replicates. Regression calibration had the larger mean absolute error of the two corrections in both cells, by `r with(rcP[rcP$study == "rc_xnc" & rcP$contrast == "RC - production SIMEX-lasso", ], paste(fmt(min(abs_err_diff), 3), "and", fmt(max(abs_err_diff), 3)))` (paired MCSE at most `r fmt(max(rcP$abs_err_diff_mcse[rcP$study == "rc_xnc" & rcP$contrast == "RC - production SIMEX-lasso"]), 3)`). It also clipped a median of `r fmt(100 * rcx("nonlinear", "rc_group", "median_clip_frac"), 0)`% of propensities, against `r fmt(100 * rcx("nonlinear", "naive", "median_clip_frac"), 1)`% for the naive estimator (nonlinear trends). Calibration within groups shrinks each group's covariates towards its own mean, and the differential error has shifted the treated group's mean, so the shrinkage separates the groups further.

## Bias-aware critical values {#sec:biasaware}

```{r ak-text, include=FALSE}
akc <- ex$ak$confirm; akt <- ex$ak$trueM; aka <- ex$ak$amend
akc5 <- akc[akc$M == 0.05 & akc$arm == "fold", ]
ok_st <- c("dgp_simex", "bihs_semi")                       # designs where M = 0.05 was large enough
pct <- \(x) paste0(fmt(100 * (1 - max(x)), 0), "--", fmt(100 * (1 - min(x)), 0))
gk5 <- akc5[akc5$study == "gauss_known" & akc5$cell == "gauss_r0.60_n5000" & akc5$learner == "glm", ]
```

After all studies had been seen, we recomputed every SIMEX interval at $M=0.05$ with the bias-aware critical value of Section \ref{sec:biasint}. The recomputation uses the saved estimates and standard errors, and it reproduces the saved intervals (5) to within $10^{-8}$. The resulting intervals were `r pct(akc5$width_ratio)`% shorter than interval (5) in the first amendment's cells and `r pct(aka$width_ratio)`% shorter in the later amendments' cells.

Where $M=0.05$ was large enough, the shorter interval was closer to the nominal level. In the original and semi-synthetic designs, interval (5) covered the sample ATT in `r orng(akc5$cover_add[akc5$study %in% ok_st])` of replicates and the interval with the bias-aware critical value in `r orng(akc5$cover_ak[akc5$study %in% ok_st])`. Where $M=0.05$ was too small, both intervals under-covered, and the shorter one more so. In the closed-form design with known reliability at $n=5{,}000$, coverage fell from `r fmt(gk5$cover_add)` to `r fmt(gk5$cover_ak)` (parametric learner). At the true $M$ of the closed-form designs both intervals covered the ATT in every replicate, because there the worst-case bias $M\kappa(t^*)$ is much larger than the actual extrapolation error, and the two intervals differed in width by at most `r fmt(100 * (1 - min(akt$width_ratio)), 0)`%. The bias-aware critical value is therefore the better default whenever $M$ is believed, but it does not make the choice of $M$ any easier. For the application, Section \ref{sec:app} reports the breakdown value of $M$ instead of a single interval.

# Illustration with the Bangladesh Integrated Household Survey {#sec:app}

The BIHS is a three-round panel (2011–12, 2015, 2018–19) of rural households, nationally representative of rural Bangladesh. We use the raw rounds to ask whether children who began receiving the primary stipend between the first two rounds accumulated more schooling by the third. The purpose is to show the two corrections and their diagnostics on real covariates. The design limits what the estimates can mean, and we state those limits first.

*Cohort and exposure.* We followed children aged 6–10 in round 1 who attended school in 2011 and had an education-module record showing no stipend (programme code 5, the 100/125 taka primary stipend) currently or before 2011. We linked them by household and member identifiers to the same household lines in rounds 2 and 3, requiring consistent sex and plausible ageing. Exposure is current stipend receipt in 2015. The comparison group reports no stipend currently or before 2015. The outcome is the 2011–2018 gain in completed years of schooling. Table \ref{tab:flow} shows the sample flow. The analytic cohort has `r big(tail(ex$app$flow$children, 1))` children in `r big(tail(ex$app$flow$households, 1))` households and `r tail(ex$app$flow$clusters, 1)` villages, of whom `r ex$app$overlap$n[ex$app$overlap$group=="treated" & ex$app$overlap$sample=="analytic cohort"]` were treated.

```{r flow}
fw <- ex$app$flow; names(fw) <- c("Step", "Children", "Households", "Villages")
fw$Step <- gsub("([0-9])-([0-9])", "\\1--\\2", paste0(toupper(substr(fw$Step, 1, 1)), substring(fw$Step, 2)))
fw[2:4] <- lapply(fw[2:4], big)
kbl2(fw, "Sample flow from the round-1 roster to the analytic cohort.", align = "lrrr")
```

*Why this is an illustration.* Among linked children without a stipend by 2011, all `r with(ex$app$receipt, children[hist15=="current stipend 2015" & enrolled_now15 %in% 1])` who reported current receipt in 2015 were attending school in 2015, while `r with(ex$app$receipt, children[hist15=="no stipend 2015" & enrolled_now15 %in% 0])` comparison children were not. Receipt is conditional on attendance, so the exposure is recorded together with an outcome-related variable (Figure \ref{fig:appdag}). The estimates below are adjusted contrasts under conditional parallel trends in schooling gains, not effects of the stipend. Restricting the comparison group to children attending in 2015 removes the mechanical part of the contrast but conditions on a post-baseline variable, and we report both samples.

```{=latex}
\begin{figure}[tb]
\centering
\tikzset{v/.style={draw, circle, minimum size=8mm, inner sep=0.5pt, font=\small, line width=0.5pt},
         lat/.style={v, fill=gray!25},
         obs/.style={v, fill=white},
         arr/.style={-{Stealth[length=2.2mm, width=1.7mm]}, line width=0.6pt, shorten >=0.6pt, shorten <=0.6pt}}
\begin{tikzpicture}[x=1cm, y=1cm]
\node[lat] (W) at (0, 2.1) {$W$};
\node[obs] (V) at (0, 0.9) {$V$};
\node[draw, dashed, rounded corners=2pt, inner sep=4pt, fit=(W) (V), label={[font=\scriptsize]below:$X$, 2011}] (X) {};
\node[obs] (Ws) at (-1.7, 2.1) {$W^*$};
\node[lat] (A) at (2.4, 1.5) {$A$};
\node[obs] (R) at (5.0, 1.5) {$R$};
\node[obs] (Y) at (3.7, 3.0) {$Y$};
\node[obs] (As) at (3.7, 0.0) {$A^*$};
\draw[arr] (W) -- (Ws);
\draw[arr] (X.east |- A) -- (A);
\draw[arr] (X.north east) -- (Y);
\draw[arr] (X.south east) .. controls (2.5, -1.4) and (5.3, -1.2) .. (R.south);
\draw[arr] (A) -- (R);

\caption{Causal structure of the BIHS illustration. Grey nodes are latent. The baseline covariates $X=(W,V)$ are measured in 2011. Log assets and log land, $W$, are observed only through the reports $W^*$, and the other covariates, $V$, are taken as exact. The exposure $A$ is the start of the primary stipend between 2011 and 2015. The node $R$ is attendance at school in 2015, $Y$ the gain in completed schooling from 2011 to 2018, and $A^*$ the receipt reported in 2015. A stipend is reported only for children who attend school, so $A^*$ depends on $R$, which also affects $Y$. Comparing children by $A^*$ therefore mixes the effect of $A$ with the link between attendance and later schooling, and restricting the sample to children attending in 2015 conditions on $R$, which $A$ affects.}\label{fig:appdag}

```

*Covariates and measurement.* The baseline covariates are the child's age and sex, household size, the number of children aged 5–15, the highest adult schooling, the head's sex, age and schooling, the division, the log of the current value of owned assets and the log of owned land area. The last two are reported quantities with plausible error, and we treat them as error-prone. We have no validation data for them, so their reliability is a sensitivity parameter, and we report both corrections for reliabilities from 1 to 0.6. Standard errors cluster by village, and cross-fitting assigns whole villages to five folds (Proposition \ref{prop:cluster}). Survey weights are not used, so the target is the unweighted ATT in the analytic cohort.

*Overlap.* Cross-fitted lasso propensities ranged from `r fmt(ex$app$overlap$ps_p01[2], 3)` (1st percentile, comparison group) to `r fmt(max(ex$app$overlap$ps_p99[1:2]), 3)` (99th percentile). Less than 0.2% of propensities were clipped, and the effective sample size of the comparison weights was `r fmt(ex$app$overlap$control_weight_ess[2], 0)`. Weighted standardised differences are in Appendix \ref{app:appdoc}.

```{r appest}
ae2 <- ex$app$est |> filter(!grepl("^SIMEX", method)) |>
  mutate(Sample = ifelse(sample == "analytic cohort", "Analytic cohort", "Attending in 2015"),
         Method = recode(method, "Lasso DR-DiD (cross-fit)" = "Lasso DR-DiD", "Boosted DR-DiD (cross-fit)" = "Boosted DR-DiD"),
         `Estimate (SE)` = sprintf("%s (%s)", fmt(estimate), fmt(se)),
         `95% interval` = sprintf("[%s, %s]", fmt(ci_lo), fmt(ci_hi))) |>
  select(Sample, Method, `Estimate (SE)`, `95% interval`)
kbl2(ae2, "Contrasts without a measurement-error correction, in completed school years, 2011--2018. Lasso and boosted DR-DiD are cross-fitted. Standard errors are clustered by village.") |>
  collapse_rows(1, latex_hline = "major", valign = "top")
```

*Estimates without correction.* The unadjusted contrast was `r app_est("Unadjusted DiD")` years. With adjustment it was `r app_est("Parametric DR-DiD")` with parametric DR-DiD and `r app_est("Lasso DR-DiD (cross-fit)")` with lasso DR-DiD (Table \ref{tab:appest}). Treated children were younger than the comparison group (standardised difference $-0.75$) and came from households with fewer assets ($-0.30$) and less land ($-0.31$). Weighting by the propensity odds reduced every standardised difference to at most 0.12 in absolute value (Appendix \ref{app:appdoc}). In the subsample attending in 2015, the lasso contrast was smaller, `r app_est("Lasso DR-DiD (cross-fit)", "attending in 2015 (conditions on a post-baseline variable)")`.

```{r app-text, include=FALSE}
arc <- ex$app$rc; agp <- ex$app$gap; akb <- ex$ak$breakdown
rcv <- function(r, meth, col) arc[[col]][arc$reliability == r & arc$method == meth]
sxv <- function(r, col) ae[[col]][ae$sample == "analytic cohort" & ae$method == sprintf("SIMEX-lasso, reliability %.1f (M = 0)", r)]
bd <- function(r, col) akb[[col]][akb$sample == "analytic cohort" & akb$reliability == r]
gv <- function(r, v, a, col = "gap_share") agp[[col]][agp$reliability == r & agp$covariate == v & agp$group == a]
gres <- function(n, r, col) { G <- ex$popmap$resolution; G[[col]][G$n == n & G$reliability == r] }
```

```{r appcorr}
R_APP <- c(0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.6)
es <- \(e, s) sprintf("%s (%s)", fmt(e), fmt(s))
ct <- data.frame(Reliability = fmt(R_APP, 1),
  rc = vapply(R_APP, \(r) es(rcv(r, "Regression calibration", "estimate"), rcv(r, "Regression calibration", "se")), ""),
  rcf = vapply(R_APP, \(r) fmt(rcv(r, "Regression calibration", "se_fixed")), ""),
  sx = vapply(R_APP, \(r) es(sxv(r, "estimate"), sxv(r, "se")), ""),
  pm = vapply(R_APP, \(r) es(rcv(r, "Posterior-mean calibration", "estimate"), rcv(r, "Posterior-mean calibration", "se_fixed")), ""))
kbl2(ct, escape = FALSE, align = "lrrrr",
     col.names = c("Reliability", "Estimate (SE)", "SE, calibration fixed", "Estimate (SE)", "Estimate (SE)"),
     "Both corrections in the analytic cohort, by the assumed reliability of log assets and log land. Each uses cross-fitted calibration, the lasso learner and the folds of Table \\ref{tab:appest}. The SE of regression calibration includes the first-step adjustment of Proposition \\ref{prop:rcfold}, and the SE of SIMEX includes its own. SIMEX uses $M=0$. Calibration by the posterior mean is a check (Section \\ref{sec:gap}), and its SE treats the calibration as fixed. Standard errors are clustered by village. The lasso DR-DiD estimate at reliability 1 is in Table \\ref{tab:appest}.") |>
  add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "Regression calibration" = 2, "SIMEX" = 1, "Posterior mean" = 1))
```

*Both corrections.* As the assumed reliability falls, both corrections raise the contrast (Table \ref{tab:appcorr}, Figure \ref{fig:appsens}). At reliability 0.9 the two estimates differed by `r fmt(abs(rcv(0.9, "Regression calibration", "estimate") - sxv(0.9, "estimate")), 4)`. At reliability 0.6, regression calibration gave `r nm(rcv(0.6, "Regression calibration", "estimate"), 2)` (SE `r fmt(rcv(0.6, "Regression calibration", "se"), 2)`) and SIMEX `r app_simex(0.6)`, a difference of less than half of either standard error. The first-step adjustment raised the SE of regression calibration from `r fmt(rcv(0.6, "Regression calibration", "se_fixed"))` to `r fmt(rcv(0.6, "Regression calibration", "se"))` at reliability 0.6, where it carried `r fmt(100 * rcv(0.6, "Regression calibration", "calib_share"), 1)`% of the variance, while its own adjustment changed the SE of SIMEX by less than $10^{-4}$. Calibration by the posterior mean gave `r nm(rcv(0.6, "Posterior-mean calibration", "estimate"), 2)` at reliability 0.6, between the two corrections.

*Relative excess calibration error.* Log land has a point mass at zero. In `r fmt(100 * gv(0.6, "log_land", 0, "share_zero"), 0)`% of comparison children's households and `r fmt(100 * gv(0.6, "log_land", 1, "share_zero"), 0)`% of treated children's, no land is owned. At reliability 0.6 the estimated relative excess calibration error of log land was `r fmt(gv(0.6, "log_land", 0), 3)` in the comparison group and `r fmt(gv(0.6, "log_land", 1), 3)` among the treated. Both values lie above the 99th percentile of the estimate for Gaussian samples of the same size, `r fmt(gres(682, 0.6, "q99"), 3)` and `r fmt(gres(220, 0.6, "q99"), 3)`. In the log-normal designs of the population map, values of this size arise at skewness between 1.75 and 3.26. The values for log assets, `r fmt(gv(0.6, "log_assets", 0), 3)` and `r fmt(gv(0.6, "log_assets", 1), 3)`, were below the 95th percentile of the same reference (`r fmt(gres(682, 0.6, "q95"), 3)` and `r fmt(gres(220, 0.6, "q95"), 3)`). The point mass also casts doubt on the error model itself. Adding a continuous error to any true value gives a report without point masses, so a report of no land is probably exact, and any error concerns the amount owned. \citet{fraser2012regression} discuss regression calibration for variables with many zeros. The estimate therefore says that regression calibration should be checked against calibration by the posterior mean. The two differed by at most `r fmt(max(abs(vapply(R_APP, \(r) rcv(r, "Regression calibration", "estimate") - rcv(r, "Posterior-mean calibration", "estimate"), 0))), 3)` years over the reliabilities considered, which is about a quarter of either standard error.

*Extrapolation error.* SIMEX needs the bound $M$, and Figure \ref{fig:appsens} shows how its intervals widen with it. At reliability 0.6 with $M=0$, the SIMEX interval [`r nm(sxv(0.6, "ci_lo"), 3)`, `r nm(sxv(0.6, "ci_hi"), 2)`] just excludes zero. With interval (5) it continues to exclude zero up to $M=`r fmt(bd(0.6, "breakdown_M_add"), 4)`$, and with the bias-aware critical value of Section \ref{sec:biasint} up to $M=`r fmt(bd(0.6, "breakdown_M_ak"), 3)`$. At reliability 0.7 or above, the interval contains zero even at $M=0$. The regression-calibration interval at reliability 0.6, [`r nm(rcv(0.6, "Regression calibration", "ci_lo"), 3)`, `r nm(rcv(0.6, "Regression calibration", "ci_hi"), 2)`], also excludes zero, and it needs no bound on extrapolation. Over reliabilities in $[0.6,1]$, interval (6) was [`r nm(ex$app$range$outer_lo[ex$app$range$M==0 & ex$app$range$sample=="analytic cohort"], 2)`, `r nm(ex$app$range$outer_hi[ex$app$range$M==0 & ex$app$range$sample=="analytic cohort"], 2)`] at $M=0$ and [`r nm(ex$app$range$outer_lo[ex$app$range$M==0.2 & ex$app$range$sample=="analytic cohort"], 2)`, `r nm(ex$app$range$outer_hi[ex$app$range$M==0.2 & ex$app$range$sample=="analytic cohort"], 2)`] at $M=0.2$. Whether the contrast is positive therefore depends on the assumed reliability and, for SIMEX, on a bound on extrapolation that the data cannot check.

```{r appsens, fig.cap="BIHS illustration. Regression calibration (circles, solid) and SIMEX (triangles, dashed), both with cross-fitted calibration and the lasso, as the assumed reliability of log assets and log land falls from 1 to 0.6. Panels give the bound $M$ on the third derivative of the SIMEX curve, in school years per cubed unit of $\\lambda$. Regression calibration does not depend on $M$ and is repeated in each panel. Vertical bars are pointwise 95\\% intervals, clustered by village, and the SIMEX intervals include the worst-case extrapolation bias $M\\kappa(t)$.", out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/fig_app_sensitivity.pdf")
```

*Parallel trends.* With one pre-period we cannot test parallel trends. An assumed deviation $\Delta$ between the treated group's untreated schooling gain and the comparison group's shifts the target to the estimate minus $\Delta$, and the interval moves by the same amount. The lasso interval [`r nm(ex$app$pt$delta_star_lower[ex$app$pt$method=="Lasso DR-DiD (cross-fit)" & ex$app$pt$sample=="analytic cohort"], 2)`, `r nm(ex$app$pt$delta_star_upper[ex$app$pt$method=="Lasso DR-DiD (cross-fit)" & ex$app$pt$sample=="analytic cohort"], 2)`] already contains zero. It would exclude zero only if the treated children's untreated gain were at least `r fmt(-ex$app$pt$delta_star_lower[ex$app$pt$method=="Lasso DR-DiD (cross-fit)" & ex$app$pt$sample=="analytic cohort"], 2)` years smaller than assumed, and it is compatible with no effect for any positive deviation up to `r nm(ex$app$pt$delta_star_upper[ex$app$pt$method=="Lasso DR-DiD (cross-fit)" & ex$app$pt$sample=="analytic cohort"], 2)` years. Measurement and trend sensitivity act on the same scale. We do not model them jointly.

*Semi-synthetic check.* The BIHS semi-synthetic design of the first amendment resamples whole villages of the cohort, simulates outcomes around a known ATT and adds classical error to log assets and log land (Appendix \ref{app:semi}). Its village-clustered SIMEX intervals had close to nominal coverage (Table \ref{tab:confirm}), but the error moved the estimate by much less than its sampling variability, so the check supports the clustered variance more than the bias correction.

# Discussion {#sec:discussion}

Regression calibration and SIMEX use the same information, the reliability of each error-prone covariate, but they fail in different places. Regression calibration fails when its linear predictor is not the conditional mean of the true covariate, and SIMEX fails when its curve is not quadratic. The evidence suggests four steps for applied work.

1. *Decide whether the reporting error could depend on treatment.* If it can, both corrections assume the wrong error model, and in our designs both moved the estimate further from the ATT (Section \ref{sec:differential}). A correction then needs a model of that dependence or validation data.
2. *Check how far each error-prone covariate is from Gaussian within each treatment group.* The relative excess calibration error of Section \ref{sec:gap} needs only the covariate and the assumed reliability. An estimate within the resolution of the estimator is consistent with a zero gap, in which case regression calibration is exact for a trend linear in that covariate. A larger value does not measure the bias (Section \ref{sec:map}), but it says that regression calibration should be compared with calibration by the posterior mean.
3. *Where it is near zero, prefer regression calibration, with the SE that includes the first-step adjustment.* In the population map its target was closer to the ATT than SIMEX's in every Gaussian design, and also in every skewed design with a linear trend and reliability of 0.8 or below. Without the first-step adjustment its intervals under-covered, because the adjustment carried `r pr(gc, "rc_fold", "calibration_var_share", 0)`% of the variance in the Gaussian designs (Section \ref{sec:inference}).
4. *Otherwise report SIMEX with a bias-aware interval over a range of $M$, and its breakdown value.* The extrapolation error of SIMEX shrinks quickly as the reliability rises. With skewness of at least `r sk(0.5)` and reliability of 0.9 or above, its target was the closer one in `r cnt_s(hi_rel)` of the `r nrow(hi_rel)` designs of the map. Its own first-step adjustment is small, at most `r fmt(simex_share("all"), 1)`% of its variance in our designs, but $M$ cannot be learned from the data.

The outcome learner matters as much as the correction. In the fourth amendment, the same data ranked the two corrections in opposite orders with the lasso with squares and with the spline lasso, because the flexible learner transfers the control group's gap to the treated units and the near-linear one largely does not (Section \ref{sec:learner}). The population map describes the limit of a consistent nonparametric learner, which transfers all of it.

Earlier comparisons of the two corrections disagree, and the setting explains part of the disagreement. In the simulations of \citet{nab2021sensitivity}, with error in an exposure in linear and logistic regression, regression calibration was nearly unbiased and SIMEX was not. In the blinded comparison of \citet{sedki2026methods}, for flexible exposure–outcome curves in case–control data, pointwise SIMEX was the most accurate. Our error is in a confounder, and the DiD target transfers an outcome regression from the controls to the treated units, which is the step through which the calibration gap enters. A ranking from one setting should not be carried to another without checking the shape of the error-prone covariate and the flexibility of the learner.

The evidence has limits beyond those already stated.

- The error is classical and Gaussian with a known or bounded reliability. We did not evaluate an estimated reliability with its own influence function, external calibration samples, or differential treatment reporting.
- The population map uses one family of shapes (log-normal) and two trends, with covariates independent given treatment. Point masses, such as the many households that own no land, and dependent covariates are not covered.
- Both simulation families of the original study use a logit-linear propensity, so they test trend misspecification more than propensity misspecification. Their covariates are drawn independently from calibrated marginals, which the semi-synthetic check partly addresses.
- The first-step adjustment of Proposition \ref{prop:rcfold} needs the gradient of the fitted outcome regression, which trees do not provide.
- Learners extrapolate poorly in heavy tails, and the spline lasso failed in one cell for that reason (Section \ref{sec:learner}).
- Calibration by the posterior mean removes the gap for linear trends, but we use it only as a check. Estimators built on it, and their inference, are not developed here (Section \ref{sec:gap}).
- The convergence pilot did not separate slow mixing from posterior concentration as the source of the Bayesian causal forest's under-coverage (Appendix \ref{app:bcf}).
- The cluster extension covers independent villages of bounded size. Survey weights would change both the score and the target.

# Conclusion {#sec:conclusion}

Doubly robust DiD with machine-learned nuisances protects against misspecified nuisance models, not against mismeasured covariates. With the same information, the reliability of each error-prone covariate, regression calibration and SIMEX can both be cross-fitted inside DR-DiD, and both then have influence functions with a first-step adjustment for the estimated calibration. The adjustment is small for SIMEX and large for regression calibration. Their targets differ in a predictable way. Regression calibration is exact when the true covariate is Gaussian within each treatment group, and its error otherwise depends on the gap between its linear predictor and the posterior mean. SIMEX's error is extrapolation error, which a bias-aware interval can carry under a bound on the third derivative of its curve. Applied work should report the assumed reliability, the estimated relative excess calibration error of each error-prone covariate, and both corrections, with the SIMEX interval reported over a range of $M$.
